title: The Effects of Generative AI on High-Skilled Work: Evidence from Three Field Experiments with Software Developers
abstract: This study evaluates the effect of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on software developer productivity via randomized controlled trials at Microsoft, Accenture, and an anonymous Fortune 100 company. These field experiments, run by the companies as part of their ordinary course of business, provided a random subset of developers with access to an AI-based coding assistant suggesting intelligent code completions. Although each experiment is noisy and results vary across experiments, when data are combined across three experiments and 4,867 developers, our analysis reveals a 26.08% increase (standard error: 10.3%) in completed tasks among developers using the AI tool. Notably, less experienced developers had higher adoption rates and greater productivity gains. This paper was accepted by Jean-Pierre Dube, marketing. Funding: M. Demirer and T. Salz thank the MIT GenAI Initiative for funding. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535 .

title: The Shift: The Future of Work Is Already Here
abstract: An unhysterical look at the future of employment. We are now facing a revolution in the way we work. A substantial schism in the past which is so great that the work we do will change - possibly so that in two decades our working lives will have been so REWORKED that they are unrecognisable. This is not just about the impact that a low carbon enonomy will have on the way we work. It is also about how the nexus of technology and globalisation will work together with demographic and societal changes to fundamentally transform much of what we take for granted about work. Why will things change so quickly? What will these changes look like? Who will benefit and who will suffer? How do we navigate our career through these times? Lynda Gratton, Professor at London Business School, is the perfect person to answer these questions. For the past three years she has worked with companies around the world to draw up a picture of the Future of Work. In this book Professor Gratton looks at the forces which are changing how we work; explains the potential impact on our future working life; and gives us guidelines on how to thrive in a REWORKED world.

title: Managerial control or feedback provision: How perceptions of algorithmic HR systems shape employee motivation, behavior, and well‐being
abstract: Abstract Algorithmic HR systems are becoming a more prevalent interface between organizations and employees. Yet little research has examined how automated HR processes impact employee motivation. In a three‐wave study ( N Time1 = 401; N Time2 = 379; N Time3 = 303), we investigated the motivational effects of HR systems that automatically capture—and make decisions based on—employee performance, and whether these effects depend on employee attributions regarding the organization's intended use of its automated HR metric system. Additionally, we test whether these motivational states affect employee task prioritization and emotional exhaustion. Results show that employees whose organizations use algorithmic HR systems, and who also attribute managerial control as intent to that system, experience higher levels of extrinsic motivation at work. This, in turn, predicts greater prioritization of metricized tasks and de‐prioritization of non‐metricized tasks. Conversely, employees who believe the purpose of algorithmic HR systems is to provide them with constructive feedback are more likely to experience intrinsic motivation, leading to reduced feelings of emotional exhaustion, greater p

title: “Potential” and the Gender Promotion Gap
abstract: We show that subjective assessments of employee “potential” contribute to gender gaps in promotion and pay. Using data on 29,809 management-track employees from a large retail chain, we find that women receive substantially lower potential ratings despite receiving higher performance ratings. Differences in potential ratings account for approximately half of the gender promotion gap. Women’s lower potential ratings do not reflect accurate forecasts of future performance: Women subsequently outperform male colleagues, both on average and on the margin of promotion. We highlight two mechanisms driving the gender potential gap: strategic retention and stereotyping. (JEL J16, J31, J71, L81, M12, M51)

title: Reskilling the Workforce for AI: Domain Expertise and Algorithmic Literacy
abstract: This study provides evidence that AI and algorithms act as complements to domain expertise, creating the greatest value when algorithmic literacy is broadly diffused among workers. Unlike earlier business technologies that concentrated expertise in IT specialists, AI and algorithms are most effective when domain experts themselves can interpret and apply them. Using two workforce datasets, I show that demand for algorithmic skills is rising among domain experts, frontier firms diffuse these skills broadly, and markets reward firms’ AI and algorithmic investments more when such capabilities are dispersed. The spread of no-code and natural language tools accelerates this shift by lowering barriers to use and allowing domain experts to integrate algorithms into their decision-making processes. These patterns underscore the importance of workforce training and organizational design in realizing productivity gains from AI adoption. This paper was accepted by D. J. Wu, Special Issue on the Human-Algorithm Connection. Funding: The Wharton Mack Institute provided financial assistance. Supplemental Material: The online appendices and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.

title: A Brave New World of Human Resources Research: Navigating Perils and Identifying Grand Challenges of the GenAI Revolution
abstract: This paper reviews the transformative role of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in Human Resource (HR) management, from a practice perspective, highlighting both opportunities and challenges and laying out a use-inspired future research agenda. This scoping review is grounded in insights from a unique Summit held in Spring 2024, which brought together HR academic scholars with dozens of Fortune 500 Chief Human Resource Officers (CHROs) and their top technical leaders to discuss the workforce implications of GenAI. The paper identifies six key themes from the Summit practitioners: GenAI as disruptive and transformative, data as competitive advantage, adoption challenges, potential ethical abuses, the experimentation imperative, and the critical role of CHROs. These six themes provide a foundation for future research directions, which are discussed regarding six functional HR areas: recruitment and selection, training and development, performance management, job and work design, talent management, and compensation and benefits. The research agenda in each area emphasizes the need for academic researchers to understand and address the practical challenges posed by GenAI. Over

title: Remote Work and Job Applicant Diversity: Evidence from Technology Startups
abstract: A significant element of managerial post-COVID job design regards remote work. In an era of renewed recognition of diversity, employers may wonder how diverse (gender and race) and experienced job applicants respond to remote job listings, especially for high-skilled technical and managerial positions. Prior work has shown that while remote work allows employee flexibility, it may limit career promotion prospects, so the net effect of designating a job as remote-eligible is not clear from an applicant interest standpoint, particularly when recruiting females and underrepresented minorities (URM). We analyze job applicant data from a leading startup job platform that spans long windows before and after the COVID-19 pandemic-induced shutdowns of March 2020. To address the empirical challenge that remote job designation may be codetermined with unobserved job and employer characteristics, we leverage a matching approach (and an alternative method which leverages the sudden shutdowns) to estimate how applicant characteristics differ for otherwise similar remote and onsite job postings. We find that offering remote work attracts more experienced and diverse (especially URM) job applican

title: Hiring as Exploration
abstract: Abstract This article views hiring as a contextual bandit problem: to find the best workers over time, firms must balance “exploitation” (selecting from groups with proven track records) with “exploration” (selecting from under-represented groups to learn about quality). Yet modern hiring algorithms, based on supervised learning approaches, are designed solely for exploitation. Instead, we build a resume screening algorithm that values exploration by evaluating candidates according to their statistical upside potential. Using data from professional services recruiting within a Fortune 500 firm, we show that this approach improves the quality (as measured by eventual hiring rates) of candidates selected for an interview, while also increasing demographic diversity, relative to the firm’s existing practices. The same is not true for traditional supervised learning-based algorithms, which improve hiring rates but select far fewer Black and Hispanic applicants. Together, our results highlight the importance of incorporating exploration in developing decision-making algorithms that are potentially both more efficient and equitable.

title: The benefits of reflecting on gratitude received at home for leaders at work: Insights from three field experiments.
abstract: Expressions of gratitude by leaders tend to yield positive effects in the workplace. Leaders, however, are not solely bestowers of gratitude but also recipients of it. Although leaders are often studied for their influence on others in the workplace, it is crucial to acknowledge that they are also complete individuals with personal lives outside of work that can spill over and affect their feelings and leadership behaviors at work. To advance research on leadership and gratitude, we take a whole-person view of leaders to understand the interpersonal crossover and intrapersonal spillover of gratitude. By integrating the moral affect theory of gratitude and savoring interventions research, we investigate how an intervention involving reflecting on gratitude received from family members at home motivates leaders to be more helpful and empowering toward their followers at work. We studied these ideas across three daily field experiments with 103 full-time managers from high schools, 116 leader-follower dyads from a variety of industries, and 109 leaders across various industries. Our findings demonstrate that when leaders reflected on receiving gratitude from family members at home, th

title: Time to voice? A review and agenda for longitudinal employee voice research
abstract: This article presents a systematic literature review of 256 longitudinal studies found from two major databases to examine employee voice, involvement, participation, and silence within organisations. We first explore the development of employee voice as an academic subject of study and then explain how similar constructs, like involvement, participation, and silence have been incorporated to our review. We investigate how the compiled longitudinal articles examine, analyse, and explain how voice is elucidated through a study over time. We find that most longitudinal studies do not explicitly place importance on the notion of time when examining voice. We then compile well-cited models and voice frameworks to explain voice longitudinally. We focus on the importance of time and discuss how exploring voice through a temporal lens will be a step forward in understanding the dynamics within an organisation. In reviewing the features of existing longitudinal research in the field of voice and applying some key components of existing models (Marchington et al., 1992; Townsend et al., 2020), we develop and apply a broader voice framework that can incorporate different organisational eleme

title: Standing on the Shoulders of (Male) Giants: Gender Inequality and the Technological Impact of Scientific Ideas
abstract: Science is fundamental to the innovation process; however, not all scientific ideas significantly contribute to shaping technological developments. In this article, we argue that, despite having strong incentives to build on the most promising ideas, inventors rely more on research conducted by men than by women. We analyze the citations that scientific papers receive in patented inventions and find that the papers authored by women scientists receive fewer citations, both in a large sample of over 10 million papers and in a smaller sample of simultaneous discoveries. We systematically explore the mechanisms underlying this finding, including an online experiment conducted with 400 individuals holding science doctoral degrees. Our results suggest that the gender disparity in patent-to-paper citations is unlikely to stem entirely from supply-side mechanisms such as access to resources, networks, and scientific style. Instead, the results align with demand-side explanations, in particular the notion that inventors pay more attention to and place higher value on scientific publications authored by men. title: Stepping Sideways to Step up: Lateral Mobility and Career Advancement Inside Organizations
abstract: Although internal labor market theory emphasizes promotions as the main form of mobility within organizations, many internal job moves take people sideways into jobs that are at the same hierarchical level as the one that was left. Despite the prevalence of these lateral moves, however, we have little evidence on what role they play in workers’ careers. We argue that lateral mobility can facilitate subsequent career advancement by allowing for the development and demonstration of new skills and can, therefore, help those who would struggle to be promoted from their current job to develop their careers further. We establish empirical evidence on the implications of lateral mobility using eight years of personnel data from a large U.S. healthcare company. Our analyses show that those employees who move laterally are more likely to be subsequently promoted and achieve substantially higher pay growth than a matched sample of employees. We also find that lateral moves are more likely to be undertaken by those who have spent longer in the job but have lower performance than those who are promoted. This pattern of results suggests that lateral mobility provides an important avenue for car

title: Bringing Worker Voice into Generative AI
abstract: The purpose of this article is to identify ways to bring workers’ voices into the development and use of generative artificial intelligence (AI). Drawing on more than fifty interviews we conducted, we identify lessons new deployments of generative AI tools can take from research on worker voice to ensure that the adoption and use of generative AI is beneficial for workers, organizations, and society. Evidence from recent interviews and past research indicates that input from workers can increase the likelihood that organizations use generative AI tools effectively and workers’ job quality improves. The evidence collected also suggests that generative AI is particularly well-suited to “bottom-up” development and use based on workforce experimentation. Moreover, we document the growth in labor union interest in and capacity for collaborating with business, developer, and academic institutions, negotiating new collective bargaining provisions governing use of AI, and educating their members on these issues. We then discuss how workers can be involved throughout the technology development and implementation process. Our recommendations outline steps for ensuring that generative AI will

title: How generative AI is transforming hiring in organizations: key issues and research questions
abstract: Abstract This essay examines how generative AI is transforming organizational hiring processes. It maps out key issues and proposes research questions to strengthen our understanding of AI’s impact on hiring. By conceptualizing hiring as a multi-stage funnel, the essay highlights generative AI’s influence on decisions about which roles to hire for, how candidates are sorted into pools, and how applicants are selected. It underscores the interplay between organizational decisions and candidate behaviors, examining how AI can shape outcomes at each stage. The article also highlights opportunities and challenges that generative AI presents for individuals, organizations, and policymakers.

title: The Meritocracy Paradox: Where Talent Management Strategies Go Wrong and How to Fix Them
abstract: Meritocracy—the idea that individuals should be rewarded based on their talent and hard work—is one of the most widely celebrated ideals in education, business, and government. It shapes how organizations recruit, evaluate, and promote, promising a fair system where the best rise to the top. But meritocracy has increasingly come under criticism for deepening inequality and reinforcing bias. How did a once-progressive ideal meant to level the playing field end up contributing to unfairness and privilege? What happens when organizations treat merit as their guiding principle without questioning how it’s defined or applied? Most importantly, how can today’s leaders recognize and fix what’s gone wrong? In The Meritocracy Paradox , Emilio J. Castilla offers timely new answers to these fundamental questions. He analyzes the structure and culture of meritocracy inside organizations, providing real-world examples—from hiring and merit-based bonuses in companies to admissions decisions at elite universities—to show how personal biases and social barriers can undermine the values and outcomes these systems are meant to uphold. Castilla provides practical, research-backed frameworks to help o

title: What Do Managers Do? An Economist's Perspective
abstract: Economic activity requires motivating and coordinating individuals to work toward a common goal. These aims are the purview of managers. What, however, do managers actually do? We outline three defining principles of economic research on managers—technological determinism, skill distinction, and managerial self-interest—and relate them to the set of skills reported by managers on LinkedIn. We highlight “managers of people” and “managers of projects” as a useful distinction for categorizing theoretical, empirical, and descriptive accounts of managers. In light of our three principles, we review research on how managers can create value—namely, by hiring, retaining, training, monitoring, evaluating, allocating, and supervising. We propose that managers apply these skills in different proportions depending on the production technology in which they are embedded and that research on managers should seek to produce generalizable insights by exploring managers’ contributions in different contexts.

title: Unequal in the Spotlight: Gender Differences in How Serving on Prominent Firms Affects Directors’ New Board Appointments
abstract: Does gaining a foothold in the upper echelons of the corporate landscape carry different implications for women and men? We address this question by examining gender differences in how serving on the boards of prominent firms leads to new board appointments. While prominent affiliations are widely recognized as advantageous, research has yet to ask whether these benefits vary by gender. Using data on the population of directors in the FTSE-100 between 2010 and 2017, we find that women are, on average, more likely than men to obtain additional board appointments, consistent with prior literature showing that pressures to increase diversity stimulate demand for incumbent women relative to men. However, serving on more-prominent boards within the FTSE-100 increases men’s likelihood of obtaining new appointments but decreases it for women. Thus, women’s advantage diminishes and eventually reverses, becoming a disadvantage, as firm prominence increases. Our systematic evaluation of potential demand- and supply-side explanations for this pattern finds limited support for both. We propose, instead, that women’s experiences of greater scrutiny and of informal demands on more-prominent boar

title: The Rapid Adoption of Generative AI
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is a potentially important new technology, but its impact on the economy depends on the speed and intensity of adoption.This paper reports results from a series of nationally representative U.S. surveys of generative AI use at work and at home.As of late 2024, nearly 40 percent of the U.S. population age 18-64 uses generative AI. 23 percent of employed respondents had used generative AI for work at least once in the previous week, and 9 percent used it every work day.Relative to each technology's first mass-market product launch, work adoption of generative AI has been as fast as the personal computer (PC), and overall adoption has been faster than either PCs or the internet.Generative AI and PCs have very similar early adoption patterns by education, occupation, and other characteristics.Between 1 and 5 percent of all work hours are currently assisted by generative AI, and respondents report time savings equivalent to 1.4 percent of total work hours.This suggests that substantial productivity gains from generative AI are possible.

title: People, Practices, and Productivity: A Review of New Advances in Personnel Economics
abstract: This chapter surveys recent advances in personnel economics.We begin by presenting evidence showing substantial and persistent productivity variation among workers in the same roles.We discuss new research on incentives and compensation; hiring practices; the influence of managers and peers; and time use, technology, and training.We emphasize two main themes.First, we seek to illustrate the interplay between these topics and productivity differences between people and work units.Second, we argue that personnel economics has benefited from exploration, which we think of as the willingness to use new data and methods to shed light on existing questions and to raise new ones.As many personnel studies use data from individual firms, we discuss external validity and provide concrete guidance on how to improve discussions of the generalizability of findings from specific contexts.

title: Mind the Gap: AI Adoption in Europe and the U.S.
abstract: This paper combines international evidence from worker and firm surveys conducted in 2025 and 2026 to document large gaps in AI adoption, both between the US and Europe and across European countries.Cross-country differences in worker demographics and firm composition account for an important share of these gaps.AI adoption, within and across countries, is also closely linked to firm personnel management practices and whether firms actively encourage AI use by workers.Micro-level evidence suggests that AI generates meaningful time savings for many workers.At the macro level, in recent years industries with higher AI adoption rates have experienced faster productivity growth.While we do not establish causality, this relationship is statistically significant and similar in magnitude in Europe and the US.We do not find clear evidence that industry-level AI adoption is associated with employment changes.We discuss limitations of existing data and outline priorities for future data collection to better assess the productivity and labor market effects of AI.

title: What Work Does Generative AI Do?
abstract: We measure how workers use genAI for their jobs in a nationally representative survey linking genAI adoption to detailed occupations and tasks.Our data provide the first task-level genAI adoption indexes, which we show can inform analyses of genAI's labor market impact.Exposure scores explain some, but far from all, of the variation in adoption across occupations and tasks.We also distinguish our indexes from measures based on genAI platform chat logs, which differ conceptually and tend to over-classify chats into generic activities spanning many occupations.Finally, we highlight that current adoption is widespread but shallow: genAI is used across many occupations and tasks, yet within most of them, fewer than half of workers adopt.This indicates substantial variation among workers doing very similar work, suggesting that understanding who adopts may matter as much as understanding which tasks genAI assists.

title: What do CEOs do?
venue: London School of Economics and Political Science Theses Online (London School of Economics and Political Science)
abstract: We develop a methodology to collect and analyze data on CEOs’ time use. The idea - sketched out in a simple theoretical set-up - is that CEO time is a scarce resource and its allocation can help us identify the firm’s priorities as well as the presence of governance issues. We follow 94 CEOs of top-600 Italian firms over a pre-specified week and record the time devoted each day to different work activities. We focus on the distinction between time spent with insiders (employees of the firm) and outsiders (people not employed by the firm). Individual CEOs differ systematically in how much time they spend at work and in how much time they devote to insiders vs. outsiders. We analyze the correlation between time use, managerial effort, quality of governance and firm performance, and interpret the empirical findings within two versions of our model, one with effective and one with imperfect corporate governance. The patterns we observe are consistent with the hypothesis that time spent with outsiders is on average less beneficial to the firm and more beneficial to the CEO and that the CEO spends more time with outsiders when governance is poor.

title: Living the 100-Year Life: How to build a career that lasts and a life you love
abstract: 'Each chapter is a treasure trove' - Carole Kauffman 'You'll walk away seeing yourself not as a stranger, but as a collaborator' - Daniel H. Pink How will you live your 100-year life? In a world of longer lives and constant change, work is no longer a single straight path. It is a fabric we weave – with threads of mastery, friendship, calm, intimacy, adventure, cooperation, knowing, and amplification. How we strengthen and reweave these threads will shape not just our working lives, but our happiness, health, and sense of purpose across a century. InLiving the 100-Year Life, Lynda Gratton – acclaimed co-author ofThe 100-Year Life– offers a practical and deeply human guide to navigating this new reality. Drawing on global research, expert voices, and the stories of four fictional characters at different life stages, Gratton shows how to: · Discover what each of the eight threads can make possible for you · Strengthen the threads through reflection, action, and promises to your future self · Weave a working life that is resilient, meaningful, and uniquely yours This is not a book about extending life for its own sake. It is a book about living wisely across time – finding joy in frie

title: The role of top managers in the public sector: evidence from the English NHS
abstract: Governments have reformed public services by adopting private sector governance models that grant top directors greater autonomy, responsibility for meeting key targets, and performance-based rewards. We examine a central plank of this approach–that directors can impact the organizations they run–in the context of English public hospitals, complex organizations with multi-million turnover. Our findings reveal that top directors have at most modest effects on hospital production. In contrast, pay varies systematically between directors but is not correlated with their effect on performance. These findings suggest that transplanting private sector governance arrangements to large public hospitals may yield limited performance gains. (JEL H51, I11, L32, M12)

title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand Lindsey
A new equilibrium: COVID-19 lockdowns and WFH persistence
abstract: This paper documents a robust link between COVID-19 lockdowns and the uptake and persistence of working from home (WFH) practices. Exploiting rich longitudinal data, we use a difference-in-differences strategy to compare office workers in three heavily locked-down Australian states to similar workers in less affected states. Locked-down workers sustain 43% higher WFH levels through 2023  0.5 days per week  with a monotonic doseresponse relationship. Persistence is driven by adjustments on both sides of the labor market: employers downsize office space and open remote/hybrid positions, while employees relocate away from city centers and invest in home offices and technology.

title: Structural Empirical Analysis of Vacancy Referrals with Imperfect Monitoring and the Strategic Use of Sickness Absence
abstract: This paper provides a structural analysis of the role of job vacancy referrals (VRs) by public employment agencies in the job search behavior of unemployed individuals, incorporating institutional features of the monitoring of search behavior by the agencies. Notably, rejections of VRs may lead to sanctions (temporary benefits reductions) while workers may report sick to avoid those. We estimate models using German administrative data from social security records linked with caseworker recorded data on VRs, sick reporting and sanctions. The analysis highlights the influence of aspects of the health care system on unemployment durations. We estimate that for around 25% of unemployed workers, removing the channel that enables strategic sick reporting reduces the mean unemployment duration by 4 days.

title: ‘Flying under the radar’: job crafting when menopause disrupts neurodivergent coping
venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
abstract: Human Resource Management increasingly recognises the importance of job crafting, which relies on personal structures of coping. This study foregrounds workplace job crafting using a critical case approach, focusing on neurodivergent individuals whose coping mechanisms may be destabilised during menopause. Qualitative data from semi-structured interviews with 45 neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms (UK and US) were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings provide insight into how intersecting vulnerabilities shape person-led workplace adaptation. Specifically, neurodivergent women experiencing menopause symptoms were found to engage in different forms of avoidance job crafting (behavioural avoidance demand crafting, behavioural avoidance resource crafting, cognitive avoidance demand crafting). Moreover, a newly identified preservation orientation drives a combination of avoidance and approach job crafting, evidenced by crafting strategies that primarily focus preservation, or maintaining the status quo, to align personal resources within maintaining job performance. title: The Search for Parental Leave and the Early-Career Gender Wage Gap
abstract: Gender differences in preferences for parental leave contribute to the early-career growth in the gender wage gap among highly educated millennial Americans. Estimating a hedonic job-search model, I show that, while both men and women experience wage growth by entering firms offering better pay and benefits, the wage gap increases as women accept lower wages upon receiving job offers from employers providing parental leave. The wage-gap growth could decline by 60% if preferences for paid parental leave did not differ by gender. It could also decline if mandating and subsidizing the provision of paid leave muted workers’ leave-wage trade-off.

title: Automation and Gender: Implications for Occupational Segregation and the Gender Skill Gap
abstract: We examine the differential effects of automation on the labor market and educational outcomes of women relative to men over the past four decades. Although women were disproportionately employed in occupations with a high risk of automation in 1980, they were more likely to shift to high-skill, high-wage occupations than men in over time. We provide a causal link by exploiting variation in local labor market exposure to automation attributable to historical differences in local industry structure. For a given change in the exposure to automation across commuting zones, women were more likely than men to shift out of routine task-intensive occupations to high-skill, high wage occupations over the subsequent decade. The net effect is that initially routine-intensive local labor markets experienced greater occupational gender integration. College attainment among younger workers, particularly women, also rose signicantly more in areas more exposed to automation. We propose a model of occupational choice with endogenous skill investments, where social skills and routine tasks are q-complements, and women have a comparative advantage in social skills, to explain the observed patterns.

title: Does Feedback Enhance Diversity in Selection Decisions?
abstract: Some organizations provide employees with feedback on the demographics of people they have chosen to spotlight, hire, and promote, hoping to spur more diverse future selections. However, it is an open question whether purely descriptive feedback accomplishes this. We theorize and show that descriptive feedback highlighting low past selection rates of women or racial minorities (e.g., “5% of previous experts interviewed were women”) triggers a motivation to respond without prejudice, increasing the subsequent selection of members of underrepresented groups. Conversely, providing descriptive feedback about low selection rates of people with other attributes (e.g., areas of expertise, geographical location) that do not evoke image or reputational concerns has less influence on future decisions. We demonstrate these patterns across seven preregistered experiments (total n = 6,502), including one framed field experiment (Study 2). One study identifies motivation to respond without prejudice as a mediator of the effect of descriptive feedback about past choices on future selections of women and racial minorities. title: Ethical Governance of AI in Public Sector Human Resource Management: Challenges of Indonesia's Digital Bureaucracy
abstract: The deployment of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) has reshaped recruitment, performance evaluation, talent mapping, and workforce planning across both private and public sectors. While AI-based systems are widely associated with efficiency, objectivity, and data-driven decision-making, their use in public institutions also raises ethical problems concerning transparency, accountability, fairness, and algorithmic bias. AI systems trained on historical data can reproduce discrimination and reinforce structural inequalities. This article examines ethical AI governance in public HRM by exploring the interaction between human–AI collaboration, algorithmic bias, and institutional accountability. Using a qualitativeconceptual approach grounded in a critical literature review of 41 sources published between 2016 and 2026, complemented by analysis of recent Indonesian regulatory and institutional documents (UU No. 20/2023 on ASN, BKN Circular Letter No. 9/2025, the ASN Digital platform, and the GARUDA AI program), the study finds that Indonesia’s digital bureaucracy faces four structural challenges: a governance gap between AI adoption and regulatory readines

title: Human Resources Management As a Factor Of AI Adoption In Public Sector Institutions: Systematic Literature Review
venue: Central European Journal of Public Policy
abstract: The purpose of this paper is to emphasize the central role of Human Resources Management (HRM) processes/constructs in the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in public sector institutions and to offer a set of recommendations for internal and external stakeholders for the adoption of AI. The study utilized a systematic literature review following the PRISMA approach in the Scopus database, analyzing 90 publications. It developed a qualitative taxonomy of key HRM processes/constructs influencing AI adoption and mapped the roles of internal and external stakeholders, offering a model to understand, support, and enhance AI adoption in public sector institutions. The study found that human resources (HR) development (including skills/knowledge development and talent management), change management, leadership, and organisational culture are the most discussed HRM factors of AI adoption in public sector institutions. This revealed the key roles of internal stakeholders, such as managers, IT and HR departments, as well as employees. title: A hybrid data-driven framework integrating machine learning and multi-criteria decision making for recruitment
venue: Pamukkale University Journal of Engineering Sciences
abstract: Context—Recruitment has become a multidimensional decision-making process in which organizations must evaluate both qualitative and quantitative candidate attributes simultaneously. While machine iearning (ML) methods are effective for predicting recruitment outcomes and Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM) techniques provide structured ranking mechanisms, these approaches are commonly applied independently. As a result, the advantages of predictive analytics and expert-based evaluation are not fully utilized within a unified decision-support processObjective—This study proposes a hybrid decision-support framework that integrates ML and MCDM techniques to improve personnel selection. The framework is designed to combine data-driven prediction with systematic multi-criteria evaluation, while also examining the relative importance of recruitment criteria and the consistency of alternative ranking methods.Method—The proposed methodology consists of two sequential stages. title: Employer Perceptions of AI-Generated Cover Letters: Detection, Trust, and Hiring Decisions
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has fundamentally disrupted the labor market's traditional signaling mechanisms. Cover letters, long conceptualized as costly signals of candidate conscientiousness, motivation, and organizational fit, can now be synthesized in seconds. This paper provides experimental evidence on how corporate recruiters perceive, detect, and penalize AI-generated cover letters. Utilizing a pre-registered 2 × 4 factorial experiment with 360 verified corporate hiring managers and human resource professionals evaluating 2,160 application dossiers, we orthogonally manipulate actual authorship (human-authored, generic zero-shot LLM, and contextually grounded career-engine AI) and disclosure status (double-blind, disclosed AI assistance, disclosed human authorship, and commercial AI-detector flags).Keywords:Our empirical findings yield three core insights. First, we identify a profound "Detection Illusion": in blind evaluations, experienced recruiters distinguish AI-generated cover letters from human-written ones with only 52.8% accuracy—statistically indistinguishable from random chance (p = 0.312). title: Skills Intelligence and Skills-Based Organizing: A Bibliometric Mapping of Two Disconnected Literatures (2000–2026)
abstract: Skills-based organizing replaces jobs and credentials with information on skills, which artificial intelligence now extracts from job postings, résumés and human resource records at scale. Whether this information is valid for the decisions it supports depends on whether research on skills intelligence and research on human resource management inform each other. We mapped 3649 documents published between 2000 and 2026, screened with a large language model audited against a human reviewer, using co-citation, bibliographic coupling and permutation benchmarks. Managerial and computational research form separate communities: only 13% of coupling links connect them, against 46% expected by chance, and the divide is sharpest between studies of the same practice, recruitment and selection. Computational research, 71% of output in 2023–2025, is itself split between recruitment technology and labor-market analytics; it validates skill information mainly against annotated text, about one study in seven relates it to outcomes, and almost none evaluate the decisions it informs. title: Productivity Without Prosperity? Who Captures the Economic Gains from Workplace Artificial Intelligence?
abstract: Abstract Experiments show that generative AI raises productivity on specific tasks by 14 to 40 percent, but who benefits when it spreads through the economy is far less clear. This study builds a capture accounting from task to economy. It links published field and survey evidence on productivity gains, adoption and wage pass-through to an exact decomposition of productivity gains in the U.S. nonfarm business sector, using the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) release of 5 November 2026 and the Census Bureau’s Business Trends and Outlook Survey. Between the first quarter of 2024 and the third quarter of 2026, output per hour rose by 6.35 log points; 3.28 points (51.7 percent; rounding interval 50.3 to 53.1) reached workers as higher compensation relative to output prices, and 3.07 points went to nonlabor income as the labor share fell to 53.0 percent, the lowest since 1947. Labor’s capture fell from 84 percent in 2024 to 70 percent in 2025 and turned negative (-16 percent) in the four quarters to 2026 Q3, while nonfinancial corporate unit profits rose 16.1 percent. title: Where turnover contagion tips: Coworker network structure, job embeddedness, and retention targeting in an agent-based model
abstract: Abstract Employee turnover spreads among coworkers, but the organizational consequences of that contagion are poorly understood. We build an agent-based model in which employees embedded in a coworker network start searching for a new job when shocks and the share of searching or vacant coworkers exceed an embeddedness-dependent threshold. Across about 63,000 simulation runs, contagion strength produced a sharp tipping point between modest amplification of turnover and a self-sustaining regime. Clustered networks tipped earlier than random ones, whereas hubs alone did not lower the tipping point. Higher mean job embeddedness delayed tipping strongly. Under a fixed budget, retention practices that reached hubs or brokers and were attached to positions rather than individuals raised the tipping point most. The model is stylized and uncalibrated, so the findings are hypotheses for empirical testing.

title: “The System Says So”: Making Sense of AI-Driven HRM, Conditional Trust and Employee Well-Being in Saudi Arabian Organisations
abstract: Abstract Purpose This study explores how employees in Saudi Arabian organisations perceive artificial intelligence (AI)-driven human resource management (HRM) and how their interpretations of the technology shape trust in HR systems and employee well-being. Design/methodology/approach: This qualitative study draws on 35 semi-structured interviews analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Findings: Employees’ perceptions of AI-driven HRM were shaped by transparency, human involvement, and contextual sensitivity. Employees expressed conditional trust in AI used for administrative tasks, but were more reluctant to trust it with consequential decisions such as performance appraisals. Concerns about dignity, autonomy, and mental well-being were closely linked to perceptions of AI-driven HRM as context-blind and overly reductive. Originality/value: By placing employee sensemaking at the centre of the analysis, this study clarifies how AI-driven HRM is interpreted in organisational settings and how such interpretations shape trust and well-being. Practical implications: The study highlights the need for a hybrid HRM model that combines technological efficiency with transparency, context

title: Gamification in Quality Control in Plastics Production: Impact on Employee Engagement and Process Efficiency
abstract: Abstract The aim of this study is to assess the impact of gamification on employee engagement and the effectiveness of quality control processes in a company producing plastic components for electronic devices. Changes in employee engagement in reporting nonconformities, reporting improvements, response times to quality issues, and the number of nonconformities undetected during quality control were analyzed. The study was conducted among production and quality control employees, divided into experimental and control groups. The experimental group implemented a gamification system, including points for reporting nonconformities, activity badges, and rankings recognizing employees most engaged in quality-related activities. Data was collected before and after system implementation, using selected indicators. The results indicate increased employee engagement and improvements in selected quality indicators, including increased detection of nonconformities and reduced response times to problems. This confirms that gamification can be an effective tool supporting quality management in the production environment, provided it is properly designed, implemented, and adapted to the specific

title: Configuring pay-for-performance plans to enhance employee engagement and performance: evidence from China
abstract: Purpose While prior pay-for-performance (PFP) research has largely drawn on Western theories and contexts, China's cultural landscape – characterized by a complex hybridity of collectivist traditions and rising individualist values – calls for a reexamination of how PFP plans motivate employees. We investigate how individual PFP (i.e. pay raise and bonus) and collective PFP (i.e. team incentives, gainsharing, profit sharing, and stock ownership) can be configured into coherent bundles that resonate with employees' evolving expectations in this culturally hybrid setting. Design/methodology/approach We collected three-wave survey data from 181 leader–employee pairs across various industries in China and analyzed the data using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) and regression analysis. Findings fsQCA revealed three complementary PFP configurations associated with high work engagement: (1) gainsharing-featured (gainsharing, profit sharing, pay raises, bonuses); (2) teamwork-featured (team incentives, profit sharing, pay raises, bonuses); and (3) ownership-featured (stock ownership, gainsharing, profit sharing, team incentives, bonuses). title: Communication involvement as a threshold resource in organizational change: effects on employee engagement and turnover intentions
abstract: Purpose This study examines how communication involvement shapes employee engagement and turnover intentions during organizational change. Drawing on job demands-resources theory, it conceptualizes change type as a structural job demand and communication involvement as a change-specific job resource. It further investigates whether communication involvement operates as a threshold resource and whether its effects differ between radical and gradual change contexts. Design/methodology/approach A 2 × 3 scenario-based between-subjects experiment was conducted with 239 working adults. Participants were randomly assigned to one of six conditions varying by change type and communication involvement. Change type was manipulated as radical change, represented by a merger and acquisition scenario, or gradual change, represented by an Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) implementation scenario. Communication involvement was manipulated at low, medium and high levels. Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and Multivariate Analysis of Variance (MANOVA) were used to test the hypotheses. title: Transformational leadership, psychological safety, and work engagement in family businesses: the indirect roles of resilience and job satisfaction
abstract: Purpose This study examines how transformational leadership is associated with work engagement in family businesses through interconnected relational, personal and attitudinal pathways involving psychological safety, resilience and job satisfaction, while also assessing the complete sequential indirect association among these constructs. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 800 employees working in Portuguese family businesses and analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). The measurement and structural models, direct and indirect associations, predictive performance and potential endogeneity were assessed. Findings Transformational leadership was positively associated with psychological safety and work engagement. Psychological safety was positively associated with resilience, job satisfaction and work engagement, while resilience was positively associated with job satisfaction and work engagement. Job satisfaction was also positively associated with work engagement. Furthermore, several statistically significant indirect associations linked transformational leadership with work engagement through psychological safety, resilience

title: Empowering Employees for Advocacy on Social Media: The Role of Sustainable Leadership, Well-Being, and Job Satisfaction in Tourism and Hospitality
abstract: Tourism and hospitality firms increasingly rely on employees to speak for them online, yet how leadership turns into voluntary, publicly visible advocacy remains poorly understood. Grounded in social exchange and conservation of resources theories, this study examines whether sustainable leadership is related to employee advocacy intention on social media, both directly and through psychological empowerment, employee well-being, and job satisfaction. Survey data from 437 employees of five-star hotels and travel agencies in Riyadh and Jeddah, Saudi Arabia, were analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling. Sustainable leadership was positively associated with all four outcomes, and empowerment and well-being partially mediated its links with job satisfaction and advocacy; together, the predictors explained more than two-thirds of the variance in advocacy intention. The findings suggest that employees’ readiness to represent their organization online rests on psychological resources that leadership helps to build, so advocacy is better cultivated than requested. The study’s novelty lies in reconceptualizing the intention to advocate online as an externally directe

title: Beyond location: how workplace resources and empowerment drive organisational outcomes in hybrid work
abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a holistic model to explain how workplace satisfaction, work activities and time allocation between home and office shape individual and organisational outcomes in hybrid work settings. The model integrates insights from social exchange theory, person–environment fit theory and the job demands–resources model to explain how workplace resources and workplace experiences shape organisational outcomes in hybrid work settings. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 10,923 hybrid knowledge workers from ten public organisations in the Netherlands was analysed using path analysis to examine relationships among personal characteristics, workplace satisfaction, work activities, work location allocation and outcomes including creativity, collaboration, performance, commitment and sense of community. Findings Time spent at home or in the office was only weakly associated with outcomes, although greater office presence predicted higher individual performance. Psychosocial workplace satisfaction was the strongest driver of creativity, collaboration, performance and commitment. Psychological empowerment was a key overall predictor, while physic

title: Reconstructing engagement: The psychosocial pathways of connection in technology-mediated work
abstract: Remote and hybrid work arrangements have introduced numerous challenges in maintaining employee engagement and a sense of belonging within organizations. This paper investigates the association between perceived proximity and employee engagement, with workplace isolation and social identity serving as mediating factors. The study also assesses whether self-efficacy moderates the association between social identity and engagement. Grounded primarily in Social Identity Theory, a quantitative study was conducted with 470 employees working in fully remote or hybrid arrangements across industries in India. Data were analyzed using covariance-based structural equation modeling in AMOS 24 and PROCESS Model 87 in SPSS, with bootstrapping for indirect and conditional pathways. A post-hoc expert evaluation involving 21 senior industry practitioners was subsequently conducted to complement the quantitative findings, assess the model's practical interpretability, and obtain contextual insights into the observed relationships. The findings show that perceived proximity was positively, rather than negatively, associated with workplace isolation, whereas workplace isolation was negatively associa

title: Present but not Supported: Inadequate Supervision for Lived Experience Workers in Australian Mental Health
abstract: Abstract Lived Experience Workers are increasingly employed in Australian mental health services. Unlike clinical staff, who can access discipline-specific supervision, Lived Experience Workers routinely lack structured support. There is currently limited evidence to understand Australian Lived Experience Workers’ supervision experiences. This study seeks to understand Lived Experience workers supervision experiences in Australian mental health settings, examining supervision expectations and requirements, barriers, and consequences of inadequate support. Eighteen semi-structured interviews were conducted with Lived Experience Workers across four Australian states, using a qualitative narrative inquiry framework. Thematic analysis examined experiences across temporality, sociality, and place dimensions. Analysis identified nine themes. Participants articulated that effective supervision should be externally provided, discipline-specific, regularly scheduled, delivered by trained Lived Experience supervisors during protected work time. Current supervision was often undertaken by line managers, causing power imbalances, conflation with performance management, lack of discipline-speci

title: Managerial Ability and Employee Workplace Health and Safety
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the relationship between managerial ability to efficiently convert capital into revenue (which we refer to as “managerial ability”) and employee workplace health and safety violations. We document a positive association between managerial ability and employee workplace health and safety violations. This relation is more pronounced in firm environments with weaker labor unionization, and becomes weaker in more innovative firm environments, when executive compensation includes stronger employee workplace health and safety incentives and when CEOs have longer horizons. Collectively, these findings suggest that while higher managerial ability is associated with greater employee workplace health and safety violations, firm environments that emphasize stakeholder protections and longer‐term managerial horizons attenuate this relation. Finally, while employee workplace health and safety violations do not significantly affect short‐ to medium‐term financial performance, they appear to harm long‐term financial performance in firms led by high‐ability managers.

title: Reskilling Versus Replacement under Technological Change and the Future of Employment Relations
venue: Advances in Management and Business Studies
abstract: Purpose: Rapid technological innovation makes skills obsolete faster and forces organizations to choose between replacing employees through external hiring and reskilling and redeploying incumbents. This article examines how these strategic workforce responses affect organizational value and employment relations outcomes under different technological, labor market, and employment relations conditions. Research Methodology: An agent based model of an organization with 500 employees was developed, in which technology depreciates skills and trust shapes effort, training participation, and turnover. Four strategies, namely passive adaptation, buy, make, and hybrid reskilling with redeployment, were compared over ten years across 48 scenarios that combine technology intensity, labor market tightness, and adversarial or partnership based employment relations. Results: Internal development strategies (make or hybrid) produced a higher Net Present Value (NPV) than external replacement in all 12 technology, labor market, and climate combinations while avoiding layoffs. External replacement achieved the highest skill fit but laid off 19% to 83% of incumbents, eroded trust, and performed wors

title: Workforce reskilling and training-finance optimization for Laem Chabang Port Phase 3: a scenario-based MILP framework
abstract: Laem Chabang Port Phase 3 is intended to increase container-handling capacity from approximately 11 to 18 million TEU while strengthening rail connectivity within Thailand’s Eastern Economic Corridor. This study develops a scenario-based decision-support framework that links throughput and rail-share assumptions to occupation- and region-specific workforce requirements and a policy-constrained mixed-integer linear programming model. The final reproducibility calibration uses public project and labour-market data, benchmark-derived labour-intensity parameters, explicitly labelled policy scenarios, and probability-adjusted training outcomes. Under an 80% workforce-coverage target, the corrected model requires approximately 1,612 enrollments under a 15% rail-share scenario and 1,739 under a 25% scenario over 2026–2027. Two-year training expenditure is estimated at THB 137.5–148.3 million against a THB 118 million envelope, while support expenditure reaches THB 37.2–40.1 million against a THB 22 million envelope. One-way sensitivity analysis shows that both financing gaps persist under coverage targets of 70–90%, completion-placement probabilities of ±10%, and support-cost changes of ±

title: AI, Employee Productivity and Performance: An Integrated ISM–MICMAC and SEM Investigation of the Pathway from Organisational Investment to Individual Output
abstract: Abstract Organisations have committed substantial capital to artificial intelligence in workforce management without a settled account of why productivity returns arrive so unevenly across employees working in the same firm under the same systems. This study approaches that problem in two stages. Twelve enabling and constraining factors are first extracted from the AI-HRM literature and ordered through interpretive structural modelling (ISM), with the resulting structure classified by driving and dependence power using MICMAC analysis. The hierarchy that emerges places top management commitment and digital leadership at the base and employee productivity and performance at the eighth and final level, with employee trust in AI and AI-related job insecurity occupying a reciprocal middle position that separates organisational investment from employee outcome. The mid-hierarchy portion of that structure is then specified as a measurement model and estimated on 412 employee responses from Indian knowledge-intensive firms using confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modelling. The measurement model fits acceptably and every construct clears conventional reliability and disc

title: Instagram as Organizing Infrastructure: New York City Immigration Delivery Workers in the Digital Economy
abstract: Scholarship on platform labor has documented how algorithmic management disciplines workers but has paid less attention to how organized workers use public social media to contest platform power. This article analyzes Los Deliveristas Unidos (LDU), a predominantly immigrant, mixed-status organization of app-based delivery workers in New York City, and its discursive use of Instagram as organizing infrastructure. Using qualitative content analysis of 102 systematically sampled posts from @losdeliveristasunidos_ny (2021-2025), the study develops three interrelated discursive strategies: algorithmic witnessing, victory documentation, and corporate narrative warfare. Algorithmic witnessing uses Instagram to document and archive wage theft, “digital firings,” and unsafe conditions. Victory documentation stages regulatory and legal wins to counter platform fatalism and build collective efficacy by showing that regulation of gig work is possible. Corporate narrative warfare names platform firms and city agencies as antagonists and disputes their public claims, framing policy debates as struggles between organized workers and identifiable opponents. The analysis shows how these practices r

title: Human Rights of Gig and Platform Workers in India: Social Security, Labour Rights and Legal Accountability
venue: International Journal of Law Management & Humanities
abstract: Transport, food delivery, home services, logistics and other app-based services have transformed the way people work in India. Platform work is not just a flexible means of engagement in the labour market: it can also bring irregular income, ambiguous rating systems, unilateral termination of accounts and lower social security benefits, and so raises issues of dignity, equality, occupational safety and social protection. Through doctrinal and analytical methods, this paper explores the human rights position of gig and platform workers in light of international labour standards, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Constitution. The Code, which came into force on 21 November 2025, explicitly deals with gig workers, platform workers and aggregators: Section 113 provides for their registration, and Section 114 for schemes of life and disability cover, accident insurance, health and maternity benefits and old-age protection. Even with statutory recognition, registration, funding, portability and grievance redressal will remain important. The paper offers a rights-based solution which includes social security, clear algorithmic management, fair compensation, occupational security,

title: Artificial intelligence capabilities and human resource management functions: Evidence from Saudi Arabia
venue: SA Journal of Human Resource Management
abstract: Orientation: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in human resource management (HRM), yet evidence remains limited on how specific AI capabilities relate to distinct HRM functions in Saudi private-sector organisations. Research purpose: This research explored the connections of knowledge sharing systems, decision support systems and smart systems with recruitment, training and performance appraisal. Motivation for the study: Prior research often treats AI as a broad organisational technology, providing limited insight into capability-specific relationships across HRM functions in the Saudi context. Research approach/design and method: A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among workers in private-sector organisations in Saudi Arabia. Purposive sampling, supplemented by snowball sampling to improve access across organisations and regions, yielded 431 respondents. Data were collected electronically between November 2025 and February 2026 using a structured questionnaire adapted from established scales and analysed using structural equation modelling. Main findings: Knowledge sharing systems showed a positive correlation with recruitment (β = 0.784, p < 0.00

title: Employment Relations and Labor Market Dynamics under Globalization and Digitalization, a Task Based Simulation
venue: Annals of Human Resource Management Research
abstract: Purpose: Globalization and digitalization are reshaping labor markets by relocating tasks abroad and transferring tasks from workers to machines. This article examines their combined effects on employment structure, wages, and income distribution, and the capacity of employment relations institutions to shape these effects. Research Methodology: A general equilibrium task model with three skill groups, routine biased automation, and offshorable tasks is simulated over 20 years. Scenarios separate globalization and digitalization shocks and compare five institutional regimes, namely market adjustment, a productivity indexed wage floor, negotiated technology adoption, reskilling, and a coordinated regime, using illustrative parameters for theory building. Results: The combined shocks moved 30% of tasks to automation and 4% abroad, and the share of tasks performed by middle skill workers fell from 41% to 25%, reproducing job polarization. Output doubled and real wages rose for all groups, but middle skill wages grew least (23% versus 39% and 43%), and the labor share fell to 69%. Understanding the Heterogeneity of Earnings Losses After Job Displacement: A Machine Learning Approach
Algorithmic Hiring Bias in Applicant Tracking Systems: Evidence from Resume Audit Studies
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Applicant Tracking Systems (ATS) mediate the vast majority of modern corporate hiring funnels, serving as automated gatekeepers that filter candidates prior to human recruiter evaluation. This paper provides large-scale empirical evidence on algorithmic bias in ATS screening using a pre-registered, matched-pair resume audit experiment (N = 3,200 paired applications) submitted across four major economic sectors and six U.S. metropolitan areas. We orthogonally randomize applicant demographic signals (names associated with specific racial, ethnic, and gender identities) and linguistic syntax markers characteristic of non-native English speakers, while strictly holding substantive qualifications, employment duration, and credential prestige invariant across pairs.Keywords:Our econometric findings reveal substantial disparate impact in initial algorithmic parsing stages. First, while direct demographic name penalties in automated scoring remain modest (a 2.8 percentage point gap, p = 0.086), non-native English syntactic patterns and non-standard keyword formulations trigger severe algorithmic degradation: resumes exhibiting non-native phrasing experience a 14.2 percentage point decline

title: Ethics at Work, Part 2
abstract: This chapter considers ethical issues connected to hiring and firing, privacy, artificial intelligence, and whistleblowing. Information is at the center of each of these issues – who should have access to it and how can it be used? The chapter begins by discussing the principles that should guide employers’ hiring and firing decisions. Next, it considers what sorts of information employers should be able to access about employees. Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to make employment decisions; the ethical issues to which it gives rise are examined. The chapter concludes by discussing the ethical status of whistleblowing, which involves sharing information that employers prefer to keep confidential. This chapter clarifies how ‘business ethics’ will be understood in this book: normatively, not descriptively. It motivates the study of the field, identifying and evaluating reasons to care about business ethics. This book does not tell readers what to think about ethical issues in business; rather, it provides the tools necessary to think through them rationally and reach one’s own conclusions.

title: Personality Was Robust to the Transition to Remote Work Under the COVID‐19 Pandemic
abstract: OBJECTIVE: The current study examines whether the transition between work contexts (in-person work to remote work) during the COVID-19 pandemic influenced an individual's personality in a sample of 1475 working adults. Previous work on personality change during the COVID-19 pandemic suggests that people experienced a significant change in personality. METHOD: Drawing from the personality dynamics literature and frame-of-reference effects, we extend this work by conducting IRT-based invariance analyses and by fitting linear mixed-effects models on longitudinal, archival data. RESULTS: Results indicate that transitioning to remote work did not affect either interpretations of personality items nor mean-level personality trait scores during the COVID-19 pandemic. CONCLUSIONS: Findings from the current study suggest that while many aspects of work and non-work life changed in 2020 and 2021, we did not find evidence that the pandemic and the sudden shift to remote work influenced personality assessment. Findings also provide support for the established theory that personality is robust to situational changes, highlighting the robustness of personality to predict future behaviors and att

title: When Flexibility Follows Employees Home: Remote-Work Latitude, Work-to-Life Spillover and the Paradoxical Role of Organisational Support in India's IT-Enabled Services Sector
abstract: Purpose: This study examines whether the latitude to work remotely is associated with the spillover of work into personal life among employees of IT-enabled services (ITES) firms, whether techno-stress and boundary concerns explain this association, and whether organisational support weakens or strengthens it.Design/methodology/approach: Survey data were collected from 104 ITES employees in Karnataka, India.Hierarchical regression, bootstrapped parallel mediation and moderated regression with simple-slope and Johnson-Neyman analyses were used.Findings: Remote-work latitude was positively related to work interference with personal life (β = .283,p = .004),while the number of days worked from home was not.Techno-stress and boundary, isolation and career concerns did not mediate this relationship.Contrary to the buffering hypothesis, organisational support strengthened the relationship: latitude was associated with spillover only when support was moderate to high. title: From safeguard to surveillance justification: The transformation of the right to be informed in ECtHR jurisprudence
abstract: This article examines the evolving function of the right to be informed in regulating workplace surveillance through a systematic analysis of the European Court of Human Rights’ case law. It asks whether workers’ prior information continues to operate as a meaningful safeguard against employer monitoring or whether its function within the Court's reasoning has progressively changed. While the Court continues formally to rely on the criterion established in Bărbulescu v Romania , a systematic examination of its subsequent case law reveals that workers’ information has lost much of its protective force. Once a safeguard whose absence weighed heavily against employers, information is increasingly treated as one criterion among others within the Court's proportionality assessment, readily outweighed by expanding managerial and property-based interests and, once formally satisfied, capable of supporting the very monitoring it was meant to constrain. The article traces this evolution through two interconnected developments. First, the circumstances in which employers may engage in covert surveillance have progressively broadened. title: Beyond individual factors: a multilevel review of barriers and facilitators to employment inclusion in autism
abstract: Background Employment is a key social determinant of health, shaping autonomy, wellbeing, and social participation across adulthood. Yet adolescents and adults with autism continue to experience substantial inequalities in access to work, workplace inclusion, and employment sustainability. Although the literature on this topic has expanded, evidence remains fragmented across recruitment, organizational practices, workplace culture, and broader institutional conditions. Methods This integrative review synthesized empirical studies on barriers and facilitators to employment inclusion in adolescents and adults with autism. A structured search of PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar was conducted for studies published between January 2015 and March 2026. A total of 2,757 records were identified, of which 45 were retained for formal title and abstract screening. Fifteen studies met the inclusion criteria following full-text assessment. Given the methodological heterogeneity of the included literature, findings were examined through integrative narrative synthesis. Results Across the reviewed studies, employment inclusion emerged as a multilevel phenomenon shaped by interacting institution

title: Not to be served but to serve: cumulative employment precarity and later-life agency among older Chinese migrants in the United Kingdom
abstract: Population ageing has led governments to seek ways to encourage older people to delay retirement using policy instruments such as increasing state pension ages, prohibiting workplace discrimination, and encouraging employers to recognise older workers as a source of skilled labour. Capacity to delay retirement is unevenly distributed and concerns have been raised about the impact of the Extended Working Life agenda on older people whose careers have been characterised by precarious work. This article explores the experiences of one such community: older migrants who have faced lifetimes of discrimination, language barriers, and institutional barriers to formal employment. This 2022 study examines how cumulative migration-related employment precarity shapes later-life work and retirement choices among older Chinese migrants in Manchester, United Kingdom, most of whom have spent their careers self-employed, running catering businesses. Drawing on Life-course Theory, we explore how factors such as migration timing, labour market structures, health, and economic, business and social relationships across time shape agency in later life as it relates to work and employment. Using a parti

title: Incentive Effects of Disability Benefits
The role of artificial intelligence in green human resource management and organizational sustainability: a systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as the technology that will allow green human resource management (GHRM) to deliver organizational sustainability, yet the evidence behind this claim is recent, scattered and largely unexamined. This study combines a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review with a VOSviewer-based bibliometric analysis to establish what is known, how it is known and what remains untested. A Scopus search (12 November 2026) returned 297 records; after document-type filtering and title–abstract–keyword screening, 97 journal articles and reviews formed the mapping corpus, and two further eligible articles were added to the critical synthesis (n = 99). Keyword co-occurrence, overlay, co-citation, bibliographic coupling and country co-authorship maps were produced, and every study was coded for the structural role assigned to AI, theory, method, context and outcome. The field is young (77.3% of the corpus is published from 2025–2026), geographically limited (mostly emerging Asian countries), and methodologically homogeneous, with 44 of 62 quantitative studies using cross-sectional structural equation modelling of self-reported data.
