title: Artificial Intelligence–Empowered Knowledge Management and Technological Innovation: A Systematic Review, Bibliometric Analysis and Research Agenda
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) now performs a growing share of knowledge work in organisations. However, research on how AI affects technological innovation through knowledge management (KM) remains fragmented. This study combines a bibliometric analysis with a systematic literature review. Following PRISMA 2020 and SPAR-4-SLR, it analyses 232 Web of Science articles and reviews published up to 27 October 2026. The analysis uses performance analysis, co-citation analysis, bibliographic coupling, co-word analysis, and thematic mapping. A core sample of 65 studies is then synthesised. The field has grown rapidly since generative AI tools were released, and 70.7% of the documents appeared in 2025–2026. Output is concentrated in the Journal of Knowledge Management and in China. The intellectual base of the field combines the knowledge-based view, organisational learning, absorptive capacity and dynamic capabilities with recent work on AI capability and human–AI augmentation. Five research fronts are identified: AI and organisational learning in innovation; AI capability, green KM and sustainable innovation; AI in KM processes and knowledge sharing; knowledge transfer and ecosystems; and

title: AI-Assisted Programming and Labor Demand
abstract: Generative AI has demonstrated human-level performance on technical work tasks, yet evidence on how these task-level capabilities are changing labor demand remains scarce. We study the firm-level adoption of GitHub Copilot, an AI coding assistant, across 5,414 multinational firms accounting for 38% of the U.S. programming workforce. To identify causal effects, we exploit a natural experiment generated by firms' predetermined software procurement cycles. Early AI-adopting firms hired more workers before the launch of GitHub Copilot and had larger, more technical, and older workforces. After one year, GitHub Copilot adoption reduces quarterly technical hiring by 29% among review-induced adopters, with no effect on separations, overall technical headcount, or vacancy duration. The hiring slowdown is concentrated in the subset of junior technical roles that involve the highest share of coding work. Overall, AI coding assistance causes firms to shift demand towards more experienced workers and roles that pair some coding with broader design responsibilities.

title: Deciphering the slow adoption of HR analytics: a comprehensive exploration of individual, social, and technological factors
venue: The International Journal of Human Resource Management
abstract: The growing importance of analytics in management, including Human Resource Management, supports data-driven decisions and strategic objectives. Despite its benefits, HR professionals have been slow to adopt HR analytics. This study aims to identify factors that facilitate and hinder HR analytics adoption among HR professionals, with a focus on the moderating role of organizational culture. Using an integrated model that combines the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB), Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), and Diffusion of Innovations (DOI), this study examines factors influencing HR analytics readiness and their influence on adoption behavior The validation of model was accomplished through the employment of Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), which was conducted using survey data from 305 HR professionals based in India. The findings show significant positive relationships between readiness for HR analytics and factors such as attitude, quantitative self-efficacy, peer influence, superior influence, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and tool trialability, while data availability was insignificant. Individual and social factors positively influence

title: Two big points from this new Anthropic paper: 1) The most AI value comes from changing the organization &…
abstract: Two big points from this new Anthropic paper: 1) The most AI value comes from changing the organization & roles 2) There is wide worker resistance to AI adoption (partially due to point 1) Changes that expand what workers do & share AI gains with them could help. https://www.anthropic.com/research/working-with-ai

title: The Five Stages of Becoming an AI-Native Organisation
abstract: Giving people access to powerful technology is one step. Building the training, support and governance to change how work gets done is where many organisations are still catching up. In this episode of the Digital HR Leaders podcast, David Green is joined by Melissa, founder of Hyperadaptive Solutions and author of Hyperadaptive: Rewiring the Enterprise to Become AI-Native. They explore her five stages of transformation, from laying the foundations for AI to redesigning work around customer outcomes, and what each stage asks of HR. Join them as they discuss: Why faster decisions and easier access to skills are testing traditional hierarchies and functional boundaries The five stages of the Hyperadaptive model, with examples from FedEx, Mercedes-Benz, Toyota and Ping An Insurance What it means to organise around value streams, and where HR expertise fits when teams are built around customer outcomes How job architectures and career paths could evolve as people move from doing tasks to building, monitoring and maintaining AI systems Why middle managers need support to guide teams through change, and what organisations risk by moving faster than they can learn How to set a clear goal

title: Residential relocation and commuting distance under hybrid work in Paris and London
venue: Transportation Research Part D Transport and Environment
abstract: This article examines the relationship between telework, residential relocation, and commuting distance within large metropolitan areas, using 2023 survey data from Paris and London (N = 583). Focusing on workers who relocated between March 2020 and 2023, it applies structural equation modelling to jointly account for pre-pandemic residential location, workplace location, telework frequency, and commuting outcomes. The results show that telework is associated with residential decentralisation in London and with longer commuting distances in Paris once initial spatial configurations are controlled for. Residential relocation and commuting patterns are strongly path-dependent and primarily structured by prior residential and workplace locations. In Paris, teleworkers’ longer commuting distances partly reflect selection into telework among workers already facing long commutes, and partly relocations that increase the distance to the workplace without increasing distance to the centre. Overall, the findings qualify rebound-effect interpretations of telework and suggest that hybrid work primarily affects transport demand through reduced trip frequency, which longer commutes only partly

title: WinWin4WorkLife D8.2 General EC Policy Briefs - version 2.4
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This policy brief examines how employers across Europe adopt and perceive remote work, drawing on one of the largest employer surveys conducted on this topic. Based on responses from more than 6,000 organisations in Germany, Finland, Luxembourg, Portugal and Slovakia, it provides new insights into the organisational factors that shape access to remote work. A key finding is that job compatibility alone does not determine whether employees can work remotely. Even where employees perform remote-work-compatible tasks, many organisations do not authorise remote work. This highlights the importance of organisational decision-making alongside the nature of employees’ job tasks. The findings further show that employers already offering remote work generally perceive remote work more positively than organisations that do not authorise remote work, while employers expect hybrid work to remain a lasting feature of work organisation rather than a temporary response to the COVID-19 pandemic. These results have important implications for European and national policy. Rather than promoting remote work as an objective in itself, policies should support organisations in making informed decisions a

title: Professional workforce composition and compensation in accounting firms: evidence from Taiwan
abstract: Purpose This study examines whether professional workforce composition is conditionally associated with firm-level aggregate compensation and benefits (CB) in Taiwanese certified public accounting (CPA) firms and whether the associations differ between partnership firms and sole proprietorships. Design/methodology/approach The study uses de-identified firm-level data from the 2019 Survey Report on the Service Industry of CPA Firms. The final sample comprises 1,134 firms. Ordinary least squares models are estimated separately by organizational form. Additional count-based, separate-ratio and incremental workforce-share analyses are used to assess sensitivity to alternative workforce specifications. Findings The joint ratio models show positive associations between several professional-service ratios and firm-level aggregate CB. However, the supplemental analyses show that these associations are sensitive to the measurement and joint inclusion of interdependent workforce-share variables. The evidence is therefore interpreted as composition-based firm-level associations rather than as robust independent headcount effects or individual wage premiums. Research limitations/implications T

title: Perceived Unfairness in Algorithmic Management Among Gig Workers: A Grounded Theory Study of Dimensions, Emotional Responses, and Coping Strategies
abstract: Online labor platforms increasingly rely on algorithmic management to coordinate labor supply and demand. Although algorithmic systems can improve operational efficiency and reduce certain forms of human arbitrariness, they also shape gig workers’ perceptions of fairness in consequential ways. Focusing on ride-hailing drivers on the Didi Chuxing platform in China, this study adopts Strauss and Corbin’s procedural grounded theory to examine how perceived unfairness in algorithmic management is structured and how it is linked to workers’ emotional experiences and behavioral coping strategies. Drawing on triangulated qualitative data comprising 19 semi-structured interviews with Didi drivers across six Chinese cities (15 model-building interviews—13 Wave-1 interviews generating 86 initial coding-sheet statements and 2 Wave-2 modeling expansion interviews—plus 4 Wave-2 interviews examined as an analytical saturation subsample for retrospective saturation verification), 38 in-depth online driver forum threads, and 14 thematic media and public commentary dossiers (totaling 422 coded raw statements and up to 482 initial label assignments), we conducted systematic open, axial, and selectiv

title: Learning from a Biased Sample
abstract: The empirical risk minimization approach to data-driven decision making requires access to training data drawn under the same conditions as those that will be faced when the decision rule is deployed. However, we may be concerned that our training sample is biased in the sense that some groups (characterized by either observable or unobservable attributes) may be under- or over-represented relative to the general population; and in this setting, empirical risk minimization over the training set may fail to yield rules that perform well at deployment. We propose a model of sampling bias called conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling, where observed covariates can affect the probability of sample selection arbitrarily much but the amount of unexplained variation in the probability of sample selection is bounded by a constant factor. Applying the distributionally robust optimization framework, we propose a method for learning a decision rule that minimizes the worst-case risk incurred under a family of test distributions that can generate the training distribution under conditional [Formula: see text]-biased sampling. We apply a result of Rockafellar and Uryasev to show that t

title: Four Futures in the AI Economy
abstract: Scenario Planning offers a way to shift the debate from prediction to preparedness. Listen to this article: A well-designed bridge is not built only for a sunny day. Engineers account for ordinary traffic, of course, but also high winds, flooding, temperature swings, and failures that are difficult to foresee. It is built to remain resilient […] The post Four Futures in the AI Economy appeared first on Harvard Business School AI Institute .

title: Assessing HR Readiness for AI-Driven Talent Acquisition: A Framework for Embedding AI in HR Workflows
abstract: Artificial Intelligence is transforming the face of talent acquisition by replacing conventional HR tactics with intelligent recruiting technologies. Predictive analytics, NLP, and automated screening give businesses more automation. Many businesses want to use AI to maintain their competitiveness, but find it difficult to integrate the tools into a productive workflow. The primary obstacles include data silos, recruiters‘ hostility to algorithmic decision-making, and issues integrating with traditional HR systems. There is a void in the academic literature about organizational readiness, the fit of AI-enabled workflows, and the difficulty of integrating intelligent HR data because previous researches have mostly concentrated on AI adoption intention or initial technology acceptance. This paper proposes a new conceptual model for a systematic assessment of HR readiness for AI integration in the recruitment process based on the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) paradigm and Task-Technology Fit (TTF) model. Overall, this paper contributes to the fields of intelligent data systems and AI-driven HR analytics and offers practical insights for ethical recruitment data management

title: Performance Information in the Public Sector: Three Essays on Feedback, Employee Evaluation, and Citizen Perceptions
abstract: Performance measurement has become an established practice in public organizations worldwide, generating a steady stream of performance information in diverse forms. This information is interpreted and used to inform judgment and decision-making by a wide range of stakeholders, including managers and other organizational actors, legislative and other oversight bodies, public employees, and service users and citizens. Through three empirical essays, this dissertation explores how performance information is generated, communicated, interpreted, and used across organizational, employee, and citizen contexts. The first essay examines how federally qualified health centers respond to performance feedback conveyed by a quality rating and recognition program. Using data from more than 1,400 federally qualified health centers across the U.S., it investigates whether receiving a relatively unfavorable quality rating is associated with subsequent performance improvement and whether organizational responses to feedback vary across performance dimensions. The findings indicate that the quality rating and recognition program primarily encourages continued improvement among high-performing organ

title: The Pillars of Islam at Work: Religious Expression and Accommodation in Professional US Workplaces
abstract: Drawing on data from a qualitative interview study exploring U.S. Muslim professionals’ workplace experiences, this article highlights how Muslim workers experience scheduling, workload, and space conflicts when seeking religious accommodations. These conflicts create moments of heightened visibility and interpersonal tension, as Islamic rituals are often read as signs of religious fundamentalism. The article also analyzes strategies Muslims use to avoid, confront, and prevent subtle discrimination, showing how they navigate workplaces shaped by white normative cultures. Knowledge of Muslim experiences with accommodation requests is crucial in an era where diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives are under fire. Their experiences help determine whether cross-cultural diversity and inclusion initiatives are effective, maintaining a work environment where similarities and differences are valued.

title: Employment in ethnic enclaves and minority job satisfaction: evidence from Arabs in Israel
abstract: Are ethnic minorities more satisfied with their jobs inside or outside ethnic enclaves? We investigate this question focusing on Arabs in Israel. Examining this issue is intriguing as ethnic enclaves are marked by minority dominancy, whereas most previous studies have focused on the job satisfaction of minorities in predominantly majority settings, and because the main theories suggest contradictory explanations. Traditional explanations for the general population suggest minority members would be more satisfied outside ethnic enclaves given the better opportunities over there. On the contrary, as ethnic minority workers are less likely to face discrimination and exclusion inside their ethnic enclaves, they might be more satisfied with their jobs inside the enclave. We analyze a representative sample of 2,209 participants, covering the years 2018-2022, drawn from the official Social Survey data administrated by the Israeli Central Bureau of Statistics, and find evidence supporting the hypothesis that ethnic minority workers attain higher job satisfaction levels within their enclaves. Additionally, mediating variables, discrimination and wages, work in opposite directions: working o

title: Resilient HR Systems in the Face of Climate and AI Disruption: Examining Workforce Sustainability in a Changing Environment
authors: Anfal F A y r Albadir
abstract: Purpose: This study investigates the interrelated impacts of environmental pressure and artificial intelligence (AI) integration on workforce sustainability and organizational adaptability. Design/Methodology/Approach: A cross-sectional survey of 272 HR professionals and leaders in Kuwait was conducted, and structural equation modeling (SEM) in JAMOVI was used to test direct and mediating effects among the constructs. Findings: AI integration (β = .492, p < .001) and environmental pressure (β = .265, p < .001) significantly influenced organizational adaptability. Workforce sustainability strongly mediated these relationships. Original/Value of the Paper: This study contributes novel insights on dual disruption adaptation in HR systems within Gulf contexts, offering an empirically validated resilience framework. Research Limitations and Implications: The study's limitations include its geographic specificity and cross-sectional design. Future research may adopt longitudinal or comparative models across industries. Practical Implications: The findings inform HR practices involving digital upskilling, AI trust-building, and environmentally responsible recruitment to bolster workforce

title: Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion Practices in Global Organizations and Their Impact on Performance
abstract: This paper is an investigation of how Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) practices are applied to shape organizational performance across global organizations through an analytical approach based on machine learning. The study measures the impact of these variables on the performance outcomes (innovation, employee engagement, and efficiency) by integrating quantitative data on DEI dimensions, including inclusion climate, equity policies, and workforce diversity. More complex models like the Random Forest and Gradient Boosting are used and evaluated based on evaluation metrics such as accuracy, Mean Squared Error and R. These findings suggest that selection of DEI practices greatly contribute to organizational performance, with the inclusion and equity being the most significant predictors. The paper also shows how ensemble learning methods are better at explaining complicated relations among DEI variables and performance results. Overall, the results highlight that the successful implementation of DEI is a strategic contributor to sustainable competitive advantage in multifaceted and dynamic business settings.

title: Adding One More Agent: How AI Team Size and Formation Shape Productivity and Diversity in Human-AI Brainstorming Teams
abstract: Generative AI has improved individual productivity, but whether adding a plurality of AI partners helps or hurts remains open. We crossed AI partnership (one versus two) with behavioral formation (calibrated to average human behavior versus customized by the participant) in a brainstorming experiment ($N$=168) with human-human dyads as reference. Two-AI rooms posted more ideas to the shared board, but human-authored ideas dropped substantially. With one AI partner, formation mattered: humans paired with an average-calibrated AI posted more than any other condition. With two, this effect vanished. Humans continued talking but converted fewer ideas into board posts. AI social talk predicted more human posts, while AI posting volume predicted fewer. AI presence increased global diversity of human-authored ideas, but only a second AI increased within-session differentiation. The number of AI partners and their formation can reshape what the human contributes; single-agent results do not generalize to multi-agent teams.

title: Navigating the Ethical Landscape of AI in HRM: An Umbrella Review and Integrated Framework of Trust, Fairness, and Employee Well-being
abstract: Literature reviews on the ethics of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management (HRM) have multiplied quickly, and the result is an evidence base that is abundant but scattered. Practitioners seeking guidance grounded in evidence have nowhere consolidated to turn. This study addresses that problem through an umbrella review, conducted under Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported according to the PRISMA 2020 statement. A structured Scopus search produced a final corpus of thirteen peer-reviewed systematic and scoping reviews, published between 2020 and 2026. We analysed the corpus in two stages: a quantitative, descriptive mapping, then a six-phase qualitative thematic analysis. The mapping shows a field that consolidated only very recently; ten of the thirteen reviews appeared in 2025, and recruitment and selection dominate the contexts studied. Fairness is the concern the reviews examine most fully. Well-being is the one they examine least. The thematic analysis organised the evidence into three macro-themes, trust dynamics in AI-enabled HRM, algorithmic fairness and bias mitigation, and employee well-being and vulnerability, and showed that the literature has

title: Unifying the Split Field: A Holistic Paradigm and Action-Oriented Framework for the Gender Pay Gap
abstract: Background: Despite extensive theoretical and empirical research, the gender wage gap remains a persistent global socioeconomic challenge, often examined through fragmented lenses. Purpose: This review seeks to synthesize seventy-eight academic studies to unify disparate perspectives and propose an action-oriented, holistic framework for future research and policy interventions. Methodology: A comprehensive literature review synthesizing core drivers of gender pay disparities, including human capital, occupational segregation, parenthood penalties, organizational dynamics, and institutional barriers. Key Findings: While individual factors explain part of the disparity, a substantial portion remains “unexplained” by objective qualifications, pointing directly to systemic discrimination, social norms, and stereotype threats. The existing literature predominantly relies on fragmented “molecular” analyses. Implications and Value: To overcome these limitations, we propose an overarching research paradigm that integrates structural, organizational, and individual variables. This action-oriented framework outlines concrete pathways, including standardized organizational interventions, fle

title: From vocational rehabilitation to workplace inclusion: A bibliometric analysis of global trends, thematic evolution, and knowledge gaps in disability career research (1981–2025)
abstract: Research on the careers of people with disabilities has grown in parallel with rising attention to diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI), yet the field has not been systematically mapped. This study examines global trends, thematic evolution, and knowledge gaps in disability and career research through a bibliometric analysis of peer-reviewed journal articles and conference papers published between 1981 and 2025. Data were retrieved from Scopus due to its broad international coverage and structured metadata and analyzed using Biblioshiny. A total of 228 publications were examined through performance analysis and science mapping to identify publication trends, influential contributors, collaboration patterns, thematic structures, and research evolution. The results indicate a steady growth in publications since 2010, with journal articles remaining the predominant publication type, alongside contributions from conference papers. The United States emerged as the most productive and influential country, followed by other developed countries, while international collaboration remained limited, highlighting geographic inequalities in knowledge production. Thematically, the literature h

title: Tradeoffs between objective outcomes and human enjoyment of work in human-AI task allocation
abstract: For people, tasks at work are defined by more than their outcome: they are colored by the experience of engaging in that task. As AI systems become increasingly capable of performing human-level work they may be deployed to tasks that people find enjoyable while simultaneously creating comparatively more aversive tasks such as monitoring AI outputs. This creates a thorny tradeoff for managers: whether work should be assigned purely based on the expected performance of the workers in question, or also account for the subjective experience of the person potentially doing the task. Most economic accounts focus on expected utility calculations based on the former. Here, we assess how people balance objective outcomes and more subjective qualities like enjoyment. In a series of large-scale (N=800) behavioral studies in which people allocate tasks to either an AI or human worker we find that people's allocation decisions are best captured by a model that systematically balances relative objective performance with the human worker's expected enjoyment, weighting human experience higher when a task is framed as inducing less enjoyment and adjusting based on the stakes of the task. title: The Invisible Harm Doctrine: Structural AI Harm And Neurodivergent Cognitive Liberty
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly mediates educational documentation, workplace management, clinical screening, and other institutional processes that affect neurodivergent people. This article argues that prevailing approaches to AI governance, disability rights, and cognitive liberty may fail to make visible a category of harm that is structural, cumulative, and experienced through persistent misrecognition rather than a single identifiable adverse event. I call this problem the Invisible Harm Doctrine. Drawing on scholarship on autistic camouflaging, autistic burnout, sensory and perceptual difference, algorithmic management, automation bias, AI fairness, and emerging neurorights, the article develops a normative account of how apparently neutral AI-mediated systems may reproduce neurotypical assumptions about communication, attention, behavior, and performance. It draws on Epistemic Parallax, a construct developed in the author’s prior published work, as a conceptual account of the mismatch between the normative frames through which systems classify behavior and the lived contexts those classifications purport to assess. The article proposes neurodivergent cognitive lib

title: Pacto pela diversidade, equidade e inclusão nas empresas estatais federais: diretrizes, governança e impactos potenciais no ambiente organizacional
abstract: Although the literature on diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) documents advances in contemporary debate, significant gaps remain regarding the systematic analysis of its institutionalization within Brazilian public enterprises and mixed-capital companies. To address this gap, this study analyzes the normative implementation of the Pact for Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion among Brazilian federal state-owned enterprises, examining its guidelines, corporate execution strategies, and anticipated impacts on the workplace. Employing a qualitative approach and a descriptive-exploratory design, the research is operationalized through a document analysis of official primary sources: the Protocol of Intent, the 2024–2025 cycle Work Plan, and the official list of the 33 signatory federal state-owned enterprises. The interpretation is grounded in Triviños’s (1987) framework, synthesizing documentary evidence, specialized literature on DEI and governance, and the researchers' critical reflexivity. The results reveal that the Pact establishes a normative architecture linking distributive equity to instrumental justifications regarding corporate performance. Its operationalization is anchore

title: When AI Should Not Decide: Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability in Automated Job Interviews
abstract: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used to assess employment candidates, yet consistent interview scoring does not establish whether automated recommendations are supported by sufficient evidence. This study introduces the Evidence Sufficiency and Decision Stability Assessment (ESDSA), which combines criterion-level evidence classification, deterministic quotation traceability and stability checks across linguistic variants assessed as substantively equivalent. We evaluated four approaches (scoring-only, evidence-aware, traceability-based and integrated ESDSA v2) using 540 synthetic interview responses from 60 evaluated scenario families across Software Engineering, Customer Support and Operations. In held-out testing (216 responses), integrated ESDSA achieved 85.19% actionable coverage and 3.80% disagreement among actionable recommendations against AI-assisted provisional references. Evidence-aware evaluation achieved 92.59% coverage and 4.50% disagreement; scoring-only evaluation achieved 71.30% coverage and 1.95% disagreement. The integrated stability gate deferred 11 additional previously actionable decisions, ten of which had agreed with provisional references. The findin

title: ONA and N1 SCA: Organizational Network Analysis and Social Capital Management
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Companies study informal relationships in two ways. Organizational network analysis (ONA) is a study that captures relationships at the time data are collected. N1 Social Capital Architecture (N1 SCA) is a description of the community that is updated as work proceeds. This note explains when to use one, when to use the other, and when to combine them. It also shows how to prepare N1 SCA records for a network study and how to check its responses against the facts. A separate part of the note covers the use of ONA and N1 SCA in mergers and acquisitions (M&A), in Sections 7–9 and the appendices: why deals lose social capital and what must be preserved; how to verify, before the deal, who the business and its value depend on; how to hand over relationships after the deal and enter the acquired company's community; why handing over records of relationships is not the same as preserving the relationships themselves. The note complements AN-13, "N1 SCA in Mergers and Acquisitions." It contains no new research data and does not test whether the method works.

title: Upskilling Without Burning Out
abstract: We are now living in an era of abundance when it comes to learning, training, and certification. There are many different kinds of microlearning platforms, including LinkedIn Learning, Coursera, Udemy, and many others. The upskilling problem today is not a lack of access. People often talk about certifications. Real capability comes from doing the work. Certifications may open doors, but proof of work keeps them open. Social proof is important. It is a noisy world. Many people claim they can do things, but few show that they can. This chapter focuses on micro-outsourcing. Use AI and small outsourcing platforms to accelerate the process. Proof of work is not limited to coding. Upskilling should not come at the cost of health, relationships, or longterm sustainability. Visibility matters. Build both an internal and an external brand. Unlearning is as important as learning.

title: Implementing AI in your organisation
abstract: Most generative artificial intelligence (AI) pilots never reach production, and by 2026 the reason is not the technology. This chapter gives engineering leaders a practical path from interest to embedded capability, drawing on deployments at Mott MacDonald, Skanska, AECOM, Balfour Beatty, WSP and Sweco and on the author’s own experience on both sides of the procurement table. It covers how to identify high-value opportunities, how to write requirements and acceptance tests for probabilistic systems and how to choose between building, buying and partnering now that an engineer with a coding agent can build in days what used to need a development team. It then turns to evaluating vendors and to the organisational work that follows: upskilling, champion networks, pilots that become routines and governance before scale. The reader will be able to assess where their firm stands, select proportionate first projects and plan a multi-year programme.

title: "Sindicalismo ante la Industria 4.0: Estrategias de adaptación y resistencia en España (1992-2024)"
abstract: This article analyses trade union strategies of adaptation and resistance to industrial digitalisation in Spain (1992-2024). Drawing on two research questions—about the alignment of the industrial regulatory framework with inclusive governance principles, and the tensions of social dialogue and collective bargaining in digitalised contexts—the study combines comparative legislative analysis, content analysis of collective agreements, and interviews with six trade union leaders from CCOO and UGT. The results reveal a central paradox: while the new normative framework, Industry Act 2024 Draft, V AENC (2023) and Digital Rights Charter (2021) opens formal spaces for participation, collective bargaining advances unevenly in incorporating clauses on algorithmic management and digital training. The Rider Law (RDL 9/2021) and pioneering collective agreements in the platform sector illustrate both the achievements and the limits of trade union action. The article concludes that a just digital transition in Spain requires converting multilevel governance into effective decision-making power.

title: ESCASSEZ DE MÃO DE OBRA QUALIFICADA EM FUNDIÇÕES DO CENTRO-OESTE MINEIRO: IMPACTOS NA GESTÃO E NA COMPETITIVIDADE INDUSTRIAL
venue: Revista Brasileira de Estudos de Gestão e Desenvolvimento Regional
abstract: O setor de fundição do Centro-Oeste de Minas Gerais enfrenta escassez de mão de obra qualificada, impondo entraves à produtividade e tensionando os modelos de gestão organizacional. Este estudo analisou os fatores que contribuem para essa escassez, seus impactos na produtividade e as estratégias de enfrentamento adotadas pelas empresas. Foram ouvidos 12 gestores e profissionais de RH de fundições da região. Os resultados evidenciaram que 100% dos respondentes relatam dificuldades de contratação e 75% afirmam impacto significativo na produtividade. A rotatividade identificada foi de 66,7%, e o "paradoxo da capacitação" confirmado em 50% delas. Os cargos mais críticos foram moldador, auxiliar de fundição, esmerilhador e forneiro. Como estratégia de enfrentamento 83,3% adotam recrutamento interno, buscam ampliar investimentos em capacitação e promovem parcerias com instituições de formação técnica.
